characters: Etse: an 11-year-old boy in a white shirt and brown shorts, with a notebook and pencil.
Pearl: an 11-year-old girl in a yellow school dress with braids, always drawing in her notebook.
Mr Tandoh: their teacher, in a cream shirt and cap, who answers with questions.
Maame Ataa: a garden worker in a green work apron and sun hat, with a trowel in her belt.
The tree: a tall silk-cotton tree with wide, wall-like roots, hand-shaped leaves and fluffy white fibres from its fruits.

narrationPlan.voice: Curious, friendly voice with calm, thoughtful pauses
narrationPlan.pace: Warm and observant (about 120 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: Light kora and forest birds with a gentle rhythm (placeholder)
culturalNotes: Aburi Botanical Gardens, in the Akuapem hills, were officially opened in March 1890 during the colonial period. Today, according to the Botanic Gardens Conservation International listing, its work includes research, conservation of medicinal plants, plant multiplication, horticulture training and environmental education.
Local plant names carry knowledge. Onyina is a Twi name for the silk-cotton tree; confirm local names with speakers before use.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
The scene on the path is invented; the story does not claim this tree or label exists at Aburi. Is that clear enough?
Confirm the Twi name and that Ceiba pentandra is correctly described (hand-like leaflets, buttress roots, kapok fibres).
Is the colonial context mentioned fairly and briefly?

teacherGuide.overview: A detective story about naming and knowing. Learners practise gathering evidence from a living organism without harming it, then learn why gardens, scientific names and respectful sharing of knowledge matter.
learningGoals: Use observation to identify a plant.
Explain why species have local names and one scientific name.
Describe how botanical gardens contribute to research and conservation.

subjectLinks.subject: Our World Our People / Social Studies

beforeReading: Ask learners for different local names for one plant they know.
whileReading: At page 3, ask learners to name three features they could record without touching a tree.
afterReading: Do a leaf-detective walk in the school compound, drawing at least three features of three plants and asking a plant expert or elder for names.
discussion: Why did Maame Ataa say all the names are right?
How could a garden help protect a medicine plant?
reflection: What plant knowledge does your family hold?

mathsExtension.task: The gardens opened in March 1890. How many years ago is that, from 2026?

support: Provide a simple observation chart: leaf shape, roots, fruit, smell.
stretch: Write the two-part scientific name correctly (genus capitalised, species lowercase, both in italics) and explain why.

culturalNotes: Aburi Botanical Gardens, in the Akuapem hills, were officially opened in March 1890 during the colonial period. Today, according to the Botanic Gardens Conservation International listing, its work includes research, conservation of medicinal plants, plant multiplication, horticulture training and environmental education.
Local plant names carry knowledge. Onyina is a Twi name for the silk-cotton tree; confirm local names with speakers before use.
localiseThis: Confirm all local names with speakers of the languages in your class.
Visit a real garden or school plot, with a staff member, if possible; do not pick plants without permission.

investigation.title: Leaf detectives
materials: A plant field guide or help from an adult
steps: Choose three plants in a safe area.
Record leaf shape, size, how leaves are arranged and any other features.
Do not pick or damage plants. Photograph or sketch.
Ask an adult or use a guide to identify them and note local and scientific names.
investigation.whatToNotice: Different plants have different leaves, roots and fruits that act as clues to their identity.
investigation.safetyNote: Do not touch plants you cannot identify, because some can irritate skin. Wash hands afterwards and stay with an adult.

factCheck.claim: Aburi Botanical Gardens were officially opened in March 1890, and today are involved in research, conservation of medicinal plants, plant multiplication, horticulture training and environmental education.
factCheck.explanation: From the Botanic Gardens Conservation International garden listing. The listing is ambiguous about the exact start (land was also cleared in 1899).

factCheck.claim: Ceiba pentandra (silk-cotton tree) is known by local names such as onyina in Twi, grows in West Africa and the Americas, and has hand-shaped leaves, buttress roots and kapok fibres.
factCheck.explanation: Standard botanical description not verified from a named page in this session.
factCheck.reference: A West African plant guide or Kew resources (to verify).
